$comment: Conformance vectors for the Celerity Binary Message Format.
A published wire format has one implementation per language, so parity is asserted
against these rather than assumed. Asserted by the TypeScript encoder in
packages/types/tests/binary-frame.test.ts and by the Rust encoder that serves the
same clients. Both copies of this file must stay identical; change them together.

encodes.name: a message asking to be acknowledged
encodes.why: every field populated, in the order the parser reads them

encodes.name: a message asking nothing of its client
encodes.why: no id and no ack is the common case, and the one a client must still be able to frame

encodes.name: an empty payload
encodes.why: four bytes, which is the shortest frame the parser accepts

encodes.name: a route outside ASCII
encodes.why: the length prefix counts bytes, not characters, so a multi-byte route is where a length taken from the string would go wrong

encodes.name: a route at the limit of its length byte
encodes.why: 255 is representable and 256 is not, so the boundary is where truncation would start

encodes.name: an id at the limit of its length byte
encodes.why: same boundary on the other field

encodes.name: a route beginning with a byte just past the reserved range
encodes.why: 0x5 is the last reserved byte, so 0x6 must be allowed through

refusals.name: no route
refusals.why: a route is what the message is delivered by

refusals.name: a route longer than its length byte
refusals.why: truncating it would frame a message under a route nobody serves

refusals.name: a route beginning with a reserved byte
refusals.why: a client would read it as a ping or an acknowledgement rather than as itself

refusals.name: an id longer than its length byte
refusals.why: a truncated id names a message that does not exist

refusals.name: asking to be acknowledged with no id to name
refusals.why: the sender would wait for an answer that can never come
